[0:06] In the middle of the 19th century,
[0:08] the California gold rush brought thousands of settlers to America’s west coast.
[0:13] But finding gold may have been easier  than transporting it back east.
[0:18] The only hope for avoiding  a grueling six month wagon journey
[0:22] was to travel the narrowest portion  of the continent—
[0:26] the 48-kilometer Isthmus of Panama.
[0:30] By 1855, a railroad spanning the region significantly shortened to the trip,
[0:36] but unloading and reloading ships at each port cost time and money.
[0:41] To truly connect these two bodies of water shipping interests needed a canal—
[0:47] a continuous maritime passage through the isthmus.
[0:52] The first attempt at this colossal construction project was taken up in 1881
[0:58] by French diplomat Ferdinand de Lesseps.
[1:01] De Lesseps had supervised construction of Egypt's Suez Canal,
[1:06] but his success made him overconfident.
[1:09] He insisted on digging the canal  at sea level,
[1:12] even though it required boring  directly through
[1:16] the Continental Divide mountain range.
[1:18] Futile excavation efforts were buried under constant landslides.
[1:23] And since the diplomat had only  visited the site briefly
[1:26] during Panama’s dry season,
[1:28] his workers were unprepared for  torrential storms, venomous jungle fauna,
[1:34] and tropical diseases.
[1:36] After spending $287 million  and losing a staggering 22,000 lives,
[1:43] the French abandoned the project.
[1:46] The United States had been considering building a canal through Nicaragua,
[1:51] but at this point, the chance to succeed where France failed was tempting.
[1:56] Panamanian leaders were also eager  to complete a canal
[1:59] which would bring their country business and prestige.
[2:03] However, Panama was still a part of Colombia at the time,
[2:07] and the country was stalling negotiations with the U.S.
[2:11] Sensing an opportunity,
[2:13] President Teddy Roosevelt  went straight to the Panamanians.
[2:17] With encouragement and military support  from the U.S.,
[2:20] Panama launched a coup in 1903.
[2:24] Within days, they became  an independent nation
[2:27] and signed a treaty to begin  construction of the canal.
[2:32] Just over a decade after the French left, the Americans were ready to dig in—
[2:36] and they were determined to avoid their predecessor’s mistakes.
[2:41] Instead of cutting the mountain down to sea level,
[2:43] they would raise the sea up the mountain.
[2:46] The plan was to build massive steel gates
[2:49] separating the canal into multiple chambers with different water levels.
[2:54] As a ship passed through each  successive gate would open,
[2:58] lowering the water level  in the next chamber,
[3:01] while raising the ship  and allowing it to move on.
[3:05] The design called for five  of these so-called canal locks—
[3:09] three on the Atlantic side and two on the Pacific,
[3:13] raising traversing ships 26 meters  above sea level.
[3:18] Operating this lock system would require a massive reservoir of water.
[3:23] And fortunately, the low-lying Chagres  river valley provided a natural solution.
[3:29] By building a dam across the gap  where the river flowed out to sea,
[3:33] the entire valley could be flooded.
[3:35] At 32 meters high  and over 800 meters wide,
[3:39] the Gatun Dam would be larger  than any built before.
[3:44] With this innovative plan,
[3:46] the Americans didn’t need to excavate the entire mountain,
[3:50] but rather, just the pathway for the canal itself.
[3:54] Still, the work was staggering.
[3:56] Even after progress made by the French, it took over nine years for 24,000 workers
[4:03] to blow up, shovel,  and drill out the Culebra Cut—
[4:07] a roughly 14 kilometer passageway  through the Continental Divide.
[4:13] The railway, now upgraded and rerouted to follow the canal,
[4:17] carted away over 76 million cubic meters of excavated rock
[4:22] to be used at the Gatun Dam site.
[4:26] Construction was only half the battle.
[4:28] Leading army officials struggled  to maintain infrastructure and sanitation,
[4:33] but accidents and diseases took the lives of 5,000 workers—

[4:40] Then, in the fall of 1913, the moment finally came.
[4:45] A telegraph signal from President Woodrow Wilson triggered a dike explosion,
[4:50] flooding the Culebra Cut and joining  the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans.
[4:56] Today, nearly 14,000 vessels travel through the isthmus annually—
[5:01] each in under 12 hours.
[5:03] The canal remains Panama’s  chief source of revenue;
[5:06] and since the country gained ownership of the passage in 1999,
[5:11] it has also become a source of national pride.
